items.question: Trace the evolution of tool technology and human lifestyle across the three phases of the Palaeolithic Age in India, with reference to representative sites.
items.modelAnswer: The Palaeolithic Age (up to 10,000 BC), coinciding with the **Pleistocene Ice Age**, shows a clear technological progression. The **Lower Palaeolithic** is marked by heavy core tools — **hand axes, cleavers, choppers and chopping tools** — with humans surviving by foraging, hunting and fishing and building shelters of branches, leaves and stones (sites: Belan Valley, Bhimbetka, Sohan Valley). The **Middle Palaeolithic** shifts to lighter **flake-and-pebble** technology dominated by **blades, points and borers** (Nevasa, Didwana, Narmada Valley), with the Belan Valley yielding both tools and animal fossils. The **Upper Palaeolithic** introduces **burins, scrapers and a developed flint industry**, coincides with the emergence of modern *Homo sapiens*, and includes bone tools at the Kurnool Caves and the UNESCO-listed Bhimbetka shelters. The overall trajectory — from bulky quartzite tools to refined, specialised implements — reflects growing cognitive and technological sophistication even before the advent of agriculture.
keyPoints: Palaeolithic coincides with the Pleistocene (Ice Age); no pottery, agriculture or metals
Lower: hand axes, cleavers, choppers (Belan Valley, Bhimbetka, Sohan Valley)
Middle: flake/pebble tools — blades, points, borers (Nevasa, Didwana, Narmada)
Upper: burins, scrapers, flint industry; modern Homo sapiens; bone tools at Kurnool
Progression from bulky quartzite tools to refined specialised implements

items.question: "The Neolithic Age marked a decisive transition from a hunter-gatherer to a food-producing society." Discuss with reference to agriculture, settlements and technology.
items.modelAnswer: The Neolithic Age (4000–1000 BC), the **New Stone Age**, transformed human society from **food-gathering to food-production**. **Agriculture** became central — people cultivated wheat, barley, ragi, horse gram and cotton and domesticated cattle, sheep, goats and pigs; **Mehrgarh** (Balochistan, c. 7000 BC), the oldest Neolithic site in the subcontinent, gives the earliest evidence of farming and domestication. **Settlements** became permanent: mud-brick rectangular or circular houses, and the striking **pit dwellings of Burzahom** in Kashmir. **Technology** advanced with **polished stone tools** (axes, sickles, blades), the invention of **pottery** (grey ware, black-burnished, mat-impressed), and above all the **wheel** and the controlled use of **fire**. Food surplus supported **granaries and storage pits**, seeding settled and early urban life, while burials (dogs interred with humans at Burzahom) reveal emerging belief systems. Together these mark the Neolithic as the foundation of settled civilization.
keyPoints: Shift from food-gathering to food-production (New Stone Age)
Crops: wheat, barley, ragi, horse gram, cotton; domesticated cattle, sheep, goats, pigs
Mehrgarh (c. 7000 BC) oldest Neolithic site; Burzahom pit dwellings
Polished stone tools, pottery, invention of the wheel and controlled fire
Surplus → granaries/storage pits → settled and early urban life; ritual burials

items.question: Examine the key features of Chalcolithic culture in India and the significance of its regional cultures.
items.modelAnswer: The Chalcolithic (Copper) Age (3500–1000 BC) marks the first use of **copper and bronze** alongside stone, in regions such as the **Chhota Nagpur Plateau, Upper Gangetic Basin, Karnataka and the Narmada** belt. Its hallmark is **Black and Red Ware (BRW)** — wheel-made and brightly coloured — while copper yielded knives, axes, chisels, pins and fishing hooks, and ornaments were made of agate, jasper, chalcedony and carnelian. People lived in **thatched mud-brick houses**, practised **Jhum (shifting) cultivation**, and grew pulses, rice and wheat. The **regional cultures** show its spread and diversity: **Ahar-Banas** (BRW, adjacent to the IVC), **Kayatha** (earliest Malwa agricultural settlement), **Malwa** (Navdatoli the largest site), **Savalda, Jorwe** (chalcedony blade-flake industry) and **Prabhas-Rangpur** (Harappan-derived Lustrous Red Ware). Significantly, larger rectangular chiefs' houses point to emerging **social inequality** — one of the earliest instances of social hierarchy in the subcontinent.
keyPoints: Copper Age (3500–1000 BC): first use of copper/bronze with stone
Signature Black and Red Ware (BRW); copper tools and semi-precious-stone ornaments
Thatched mud-brick houses; Jhum (shifting) cultivation; pulses, rice, wheat
Regional cultures: Ahar-Banas, Kayatha, Malwa, Savalda, Jorwe, Prabhas-Rangpur
Large chiefs' houses — early evidence of social inequality/hierarchy
